summary: Second independent verification of flow 003 at 1ed5b2a, run entirely in a detached worktree at /tmp/echolet-verify-r2 (created because two other agents were changing the main tree; removed afterwards). Node v26.5.0 measured, every Go leg with -count=1 and none cached. THE MATRIX: typecheck exit 0; pnpm -r test exit 0 with 66 files / 338 tests / 0 failed / 0 skipped; Go untagged, -race and -race -tags relayv2 all exit 0 with 175 RUN / 175 PASS / 0 FAIL / 0 SKIP and ZERO data races in all three; test:e2e exit 0 on an idle host with 7 files / 30 tests in 885 s - but exit 143 with ELEVEN E2E-child-timeout failures on its first run, which is R2-004. WHAT I RE-ESTABLISHED RATHER THAN READ: all three new mutation-killed tests kill their mutations when I run them (the trust-modal viewport guard, 3 of 5 tests, one per axis of the disjunction; the TypeScript/Go size mirror, in both directions; the cleanup-service Stop join, with internal/server still ok). The reservation property survives a DIRECT attack I wrote myself: 80 concurrent claims against a 20-member pool serve exactly 20, with 20 distinct bundle ids and 20 distinct one-time prekeys, over 5/5 runs under -race with 0 races - and the wave's own green regression pin is NOT vacuous, since re-adding the availability index on an idempotent re-publish makes it fail. Seven mutations, all killed, all reverted; the whole-tree SHA-256 manifest is identical before and after (883e5323..., 1010 files). No test is weakened, skipped, narrowed or deleted: every corrected count is an exact toEqual/toHaveLength derived from LIMITS.PREKEY_MIN_COUNT, the off-by-one is diagnosed on the correct side (N-1 = 19, cross-checked against step 6's own pool.claimable assertion), and all fifteen recorded digests match the committed tree byte-for-byte. THE POOL'S COST, MEASURED: the headline 120 -> 6 victims per minute is HONEST (120/min per-host limit applied as global middleware, one claim per member). Two subsidiary claims are not. A full-drain publish costs 40 requests, not the 20 and 17 % the design states (measured 20 / 20 / 21 / 40 for empty / steady / one-dead-slot / full-drain), and 'two source addresses drain a pool faster than its owner can refill it' is optimistic by 2x: one source destroys 120 members/min against a recovery ceiling of 60. T31's report already corrects the first; the design and an e2e comment were never updated. VERDICTS: AC4, AC5, AC6, AC7, AC8 and AC9 MET (AC9 now genuinely pinned, V-001 closed); AC3 and AC10 PARTIAL; AC1 and AC2 NOT MET. AC2 fails on the design's OWN enumerated list: 9 of the 11 sites t26 said must be edited in the same change are unedited, and 1ed5b2a touched no file under docs/. And the push gate has a state it passes that it should stop: its two blocking steps test the WORKING TREE, so a scratch repo with a red committed suite and a green uncommitted tree pushes clean at gate exit 0 - not weaker than what it replaced, but not what its own header claims, and unreachable by all 27 self-test rows because each builds the tree equal to HEAD.

findings.problem: The two BLOCKING gate steps - the Go suite and `keryx test run --strict` - run against the WORKING TREE, not against the commits being pushed. Only step 1 (security scan) and step 4 (documentation pin) consume the ref lines git puts on stdin. The hook's own header (lines 105-107) claims the opposite: that reading stdin 'lets the gate ask about the commits actually being pushed rather than about the working tree - which is the mistake that made the old gate pass vacuously'.
findings.impact: A commit whose suite is red can be pushed, verified green, whenever the working tree differs from it: commit, notice the break, fix locally without committing, push. Also hit by pushing an older branch tip while the tree carries newer code. The 27-row self-test cannot see this state, because every row is built with the working tree equal to HEAD. The gate is still not WEAKER than the stock keryx hook (`--changed` was working-tree-scoped too), so the 'strictly no weaker' claim survives - the range-awareness claim and the completeness of the state table do not.
findings.suggested_fix: Either run the test steps against a checkout of the pushed tip (git worktree add at ECHOLET_PUSH_TIP, install, run there, remove) or, at minimum, block when `git status --porcelain` is non-empty during a push, and correct the header comment so it stops claiming range-awareness the test steps do not have. Add the dirty-tree row to scripts/gate/selftest.sh.

findings.symbol: Cost of N = 20, measured rather than guessed
findings.problem: The design states 'A full-drain relay publish: 20 x 61.6 ms ~ 1.23 s, and 20 requests - 17 % of the shipped 120/min budget', and 2.3 says six publishes a minute hit the limiter. The implemented loop - the loop the design itself specifies - re-submits every stored member AND publishes one replacement per dead slot, so the cost is N + k and a full drain is 2N. Measured: 40 requests, 33 % of the budget, three publishes to hit the limiter. t31-implementation-report.md 4.5 catches this and states it correctly; the design was never corrected, and test/e2e/prekey-pool-replenishment.test.ts:121-123 still tells the next reader that at N = 20 one relay publish is 20 requests.
findings.impact: The cost model a reader will quote is the design's, and it understates the defender's per-recovery request budget by 2x - exactly the half of the analysis that decides whether the recovery path can keep up with the attack.
findings.suggested_fix: Correct t26-replenishment-design.md:157 and 2.3 to N + k / 2N / 33 % / three, and correct the comment at prekey-pool-replenishment.test.ts:121-123, which is also the stated justification for raising ECHOLET_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE to 100000 in that test.
findings.evidence: Instrumented the real publish() loop against the suite's own fake relay (probe appended to outbound.publicationPool.test.ts, run, reverted; sha256 d7a8db80... before and after): first publish 20, steady state 20, one dead slot 21, FULL-DRAIN top-up 40 with minted = 20. Matches outbound.publicationPool.test.ts's own B-7 shape (20 resubmissions plus 3 mints for 3 consumed).

findings.problem: 'Two source addresses drain a pool faster than its owner can refill it' (also PAUSED.md:20 and the T26 design). With the measured 2 requests per restored member at full drain against 1 request per destroyed member, and the shipped 120 requests/minute keyed on the peer host, ONE attacking source destroys 120 members/minute while one recovering victim restores at most 60/minute - and as few as ~5.7/minute if the pool is drained a member at a time, since a single dead slot still costs 21 requests. One source already out-drains the owner by at least 2:1.
findings.impact: The sentence sits in the file whose stated purpose is the honest cost, and it overstates the defence by a factor of two in the defender's favour. The headline it accompanies (120 -> 6 victims/minute) is correct; this one is not, and it is the claim that decides whether the recovery path is sustainable under a targeted attack.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with the measured statement: one source at the shipped rate limit destroys members twice as fast as the owner can restore them, so the pool buys a 20x breadth reduction and a one-shot recovery, not a sustainable defence against a targeted attacker.
findings.evidence: middleware/rate_limit.go (per-host quota; global r.Use at router.go:47; default 120 at config.go:57 and geekom.env.example:62) with the measured 40-request full-drain and 21-request single-slot top-ups from R2-005's probe.

findings.problem: The recovery path has a finite total budget the design costs only in the benign case. maxOneTimePreKeyId = 0xffffff (16 777 215), rotateOneTimePreKey() is strictly increasing, and the design explicitly forbids any pool GC, so consumed pre: records accumulate for the life of the profile. t26 2.2 computes '~16 000 centuries' from 20 ids per week. Under the attack the pool exists to price, the burn rate is the recovery rate: ~60 ids/minute sustained from one source exhausts the space in ~194 days, after which rotateOneTimePreKey() throws 'One-time prekey identifiers are exhausted' and relay publish fails permanently.
findings.impact: Slow, bounded, and far outside a prototype's horizon - but it is the one place the recovery path can be destroyed outright rather than merely outpaced, and the design's adversarial section does not carry the adversarial figure.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the adversarial figure beside the benign one, and note that bounded retention for consumed pre: records - which must never prune a record a claim may still be outstanding against - is a follow-on rather than a non-issue.

findings.problem: pnpm install inside ANY git worktree runs the root prepare script, which resolves its hook target as git rev-parse --git-common-dir - from a worktree that is the MAIN repository's .git - and writes git config core.hooksPath, which is also shared across worktrees. Installing dependencies in a throwaway worktree therefore rewrites the parent repository's .git/hooks/pre-push and can change the parent's hook configuration.
findings.impact: Nothing tracked changes and the rewrite is idempotent by design, so the blast radius is small. But an agent or a developer creating a worktree specifically to avoid touching the main checkout will silently touch it anyway. Observed in this verification run: the install reported 'core.hooksPath tripwire refreshed in .../echolet/.git/hooks/pre-push' and 'core.hooksPath = .githooks' with no '(was: ...)' clause, so the config value was already correct and I did not change it.
findings.suggested_fix: Either say so in the script's header, or skip the tripwire refresh when git rev-parse --git-dir differs from --git-common-dir, i.e. when running inside a linked worktree.
